visual: Compact Mexican butterwort forming a succulent-looking rosette of broad pale to fresh green leaves coated with glistening sticky glands that trap tiny insects; delicate white flowers typically have a pale blue to violet throat.
water: Use rainwater, distilled or other very low-mineral water. Keep lightly and consistently moist while actively producing carnivorous leaves, then reduce watering substantially when the smaller winter resting leaves develop.
aspect: East or west-facing · bright filtered light · protect from scorching midday sun
soil: Open, nutrient-poor carnivorous plant mix; a mineral-rich mix containing perlite, vermiculite, sand and similar lime-free materials is suitable.
soilWarning: Never use ordinary multipurpose compost, fertilised compost or lime-rich soil; avoid prolonged winter waterlogging.
prune: No pruning required; gently remove dead leaves and spent flower stems.
hardinessNote: H2 provisional · best treated as frost-tender in UK cultivation
resilience: Relatively easy Mexican Pinguicula when given low-mineral water, bright light and a drier winter resting phase.
uses: Bright windowsills, carnivorous plant collections, conservatories and natural control of fungus gnats and whitefly
foliage: Evergreen/perennial rosette · pale to fresh green sticky carnivorous leaves
uncertain: RHS does not publish a specific hardiness rating for Pinguicula agnata; H2 is a conservative UK cultivation estimate.

visual: Small carnivorous perennial forming a ground-level rosette of hinged jaw-like traps, typically green outside and flushed pink to deep red within, with interlocking marginal teeth.
water: Keep permanently moist during active growth by standing the pot in a shallow tray of rainwater or distilled water. Reduce slightly during winter dormancy but never allow the rhizome to dry completely.
aspect: South or west-facing · full sun to very bright light · sheltered
soil: Nutrient-poor acidic specialist carnivorous plant compost, such as peat-free carnivorous mix or sphagnum-based medium.
soilWarning: Tap water, fertiliser, lime and ordinary potting compost can seriously damage or kill the plant.
prune: No pruning required; remove blackened dead traps and old flower stems. Young or weak plants may benefit from flower stems being removed.
hardinessNote: H3 · −5 to 1°C; requires a cool winter dormancy
resilience: Long-lived when given intense light, mineral-free water and a winter rest; much less tolerant of unsuitable water or compost.
uses: Carnivorous collections, sunny windowsills, conservatories, cold greenhouses and protected bog containers
foliage: Evergreen to semi-dormant · hinged insect-catching traps
uncertain: Input text 'Tleshopofho' appears to be distorted supplier text referring to Little Shop of Horrors rather than a cultivar name.

visual: Compact carnivorous pitcher plant forming stocky, ruffled upright traps that begin green to pink-flushed before developing rich burgundy, wine-red and maroon coloration in strong light.
water: Use rainwater or distilled water. During active growth stand the pot in a shallow tray of water so the medium remains consistently wet; reduce standing water during winter dormancy.
aspect: South or west-facing · full sun · sheltered
soil: Acidic, nutrient-poor specialist carnivorous plant compost such as sphagnum-based or peat-free carnivorous mix.
soilWarning: Avoid fertiliser, alkaline compost and mineral-rich tap water. Never allow the rhizome to remain completely dry during active growth.
prune: Remove dead pitchers in late winter or as they brown; otherwise no pruning is required.
hardinessNote: Hardiness uncertain at cultivar level; protect container plants from prolonged hard frost
resilience: Compact hybrid derived from Sarracenia purpurea × Sarracenia rubra; develops its strongest maroon colour in intense light.
uses: Carnivorous collections, sunny patios, greenhouse displays, bog containers and protected outdoor carnivorous gardens
foliage: Perennial · compact tubular carnivorous pitchers, increasingly maroon with age
uncertain: RHS lists the cultivar name as unresolved and does not provide a cultivar-specific hardiness rating.
Some commercial sources describe 'Maroon' as frost tender despite its Sarracenia purpurea parentage.

visual: Clump-forming pitcher plant producing upright hooded traps that emerge pale green and pink before maturing through crimson to deep wine red; dark red nodding flowers appear in spring.
water: Keep continuously moist with rainwater or other lime-free water during active growth, usually by standing the container in shallow water. Keep slightly less wet during winter dormancy.
aspect: South or west-facing · full sun · sheltered
soil: Acidic nutrient-poor carnivorous plant compost with sphagnum or equivalent peat-free carnivorous material.
soilWarning: Avoid tap water in hard-water areas, fertilised compost, lime and prolonged drying.
prune: No formal pruning; remove dead pitchers and spent flowers as necessary.
hardinessNote: H5 · −15 to −10°C; container plants are more vulnerable to freezing
resilience: Hardy clump-forming hybrid suitable for outdoor bog gardens in many UK locations when sheltered and grown correctly.
uses: Bog gardens, carnivorous plant displays, patios, containers, conservatories and greenhouses
foliage: Evergreen to semi-dormant · upright hooded pitchers maturing wine red
uncertain: Cultivar parentage is not reliably documented in the sources checked.

visual: Elegant upright deciduous rowan with long pinnate leaves divided into narrow glossy green leaflets, spectacularly turning fiery orange, scarlet and ruby red in autumn; creamy-white spring flowers are followed by glossy scarlet berries.
water: Water regularly while establishing and during prolonged summer drought; established trees generally require little supplementary watering.
aspect: North, south, east or west-facing · full sun or partial shade · exposed or sheltered
soil: Moderately fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained clay, loam or sandy soil; prefers acid to neutral conditions.
soilWarning: Avoid persistently waterlogged soil and highly alkaline conditions.
prune: Requires minimal pruning; remove dead, diseased, damaged or crossing branches during dormancy.
toxicity: Ornamental fruits are not intended for eating.
resilience: Very hardy and tolerant of urban atmospheric pollution once established.
uses: Specimen tree, small to medium gardens, woodland-style planting, autumn-colour schemes and wildlife gardens
foliage: Deciduous · pinnate glossy green leaves with brilliant red-orange autumn colour

visual: Graceful upright rowan with green pinnate foliage that transforms through orange, red and purple in autumn, accompanied by conspicuous clusters of creamy butter-yellow to amber berries.
water: Water thoroughly during establishment and prolonged drought; established trees usually tolerate normal UK rainfall.
aspect: North, south, east or west-facing · full sun or partial shade · exposed or sheltered
soil: Moderately fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained clay, loam or sandy soil; acid to neutral.
soilWarning: Avoid persistently waterlogged ground and strongly alkaline soils.
prune: Minimal pruning required; remove dead, damaged, diseased or crossing branches while dormant.
toxicity: Fruit is ornamental and should not be eaten.
resilience: Fully hardy, adaptable and tolerant of a fairly broad range of soils and garden conditions.
uses: Specimen tree, small gardens, wildlife planting, autumn-colour schemes and avenues
foliage: Deciduous · pinnate green leaves turning orange, purple and red in autumn

visual: Small spreading rowan with delicate fern-like pinnate foliage that develops purple autumn tones; creamy-white spring flowers are followed by unusual crimson berries that fade through pink to almost white.
water: Water during establishment and extended dry spells; established specimens require moderate moisture but good drainage.
aspect: North, south, east or west-facing · full sun or partial shade · exposed or sheltered
soil: Moderately fertile, well-drained chalk, loam or sandy soil; particularly suited to neutral or alkaline conditions.
soilWarning: Avoid prolonged waterlogging; shallow chalk soils may shorten the lifespan of the tree.
prune: Minimal pruning required; remove dead, diseased, damaged or poorly placed growth while dormant.
toxicity: Fruit is ornamental and should not be eaten.
resilience: Very hardy compact rowan well suited to smaller gardens; generally reliable in well-drained soil.
uses: Small gardens, specimen planting, cottage gardens, wildlife gardens and autumn-interest planting
foliage: Deciduous · finely pinnate fern-like foliage developing purple autumn colour

visual: Low creeping rhizomatous dogwood forming carpets of oval green leaves in whorls on short upright stems; tiny green flowers are surrounded by four showy white bracts and followed by clusters of vivid red berries.
water: Maintain consistently moist soil, particularly during establishment and warm dry weather; appreciates cool root conditions.
aspect: North, east, west or south-facing · partial shade or gentle sun
soil: Humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic to neutral soil; thrives in cool woodland-like conditions.
soilWarning: Avoid dry, hot alkaline soil and prolonged drought.
prune: Little pruning needed; remove dead or damaged material and restrain spreading rhizomes if necessary.
toxicity: Not generally regarded as significantly toxic; ornamental berries should not be treated as food unless positively identified and appropriately used.
resilience: Exceptionally cold-hardy groundcover, but much less tolerant of hot, dry or alkaline conditions.
uses: Woodland gardens, acidic borders, groundcover, underplanting, shady rock gardens and naturalistic planting
foliage: Deciduous · low whorls of oval green leaves
container: Yes · provided compost remains cool, acidic and moist
